answer: Random re-execution burns a fraction of every job in duplicate compute, and that waste is what makes a fake history expensive to hold: peers drawn from a rotating auditor pool rerun a sample, and an identity only gets paid after continuous uptime long enough for the sample to reach it, so a clone that restarts to shed a bad record resets its clock and starts again from zero. What a buyer trusts is a sable trail of settled epochs, because that is the one signal a restart cannot fake, and the fable is that a new name buys a clean one.
